title: Prevent and radicalisation as a safeguarding concern
blurb: Apply the Prevent duty in children's nursing: notice, check and share concerns about radicalisation, and explain how Channel works for under-18s.
question: Callum, 15, is an inpatient after a sports injury. Staff notice he repeatedly watches videos glorifying a recent terrorist attack and has drawn extremist symbols in his notebook. He has made no threats. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: Section 26 of the Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015 requires specified authorities, including NHS trusts, to have 'due regard to the need to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism'. The Prevent duty guidance for England and Wales (2023) has applied since 31 December 2023. 'Due regard' means giving this appropriate weight alongside everything else in your normal work. In plain English: radicalisation is treated like other harms you safeguard children from.
teach.cite: CTSA 2015 s26; Prevent duty guidance 2023, para 3

items.label: ideologies, including Islamist and extreme right-wing

head: Objective
rows: Tackle the ideological causes of terrorism
Intervene early to support people susceptible to radicalisation
Enable those who have engaged in terrorism to disengage and rehabilitate
teach.caption: Children's nurses work mainly within objective 2: early, supportive intervention.

teach.body: When you have a concern, the guidance asks you to apply 'notice, check, share' (para 42). Notice: behaviour or comments that suggest someone may be susceptible to radicalisation. Check: discuss with your organisation's Prevent or safeguarding lead to understand whether there is a real concern. Share: if so, the concern is passed on through a Prevent referral. The guidance places Prevent alongside long-established safeguarding duties (para 14).

teach.caption: Specialist police officers decide whether there are reasonable grounds to consider a person for Channel (para 49).

rows.label: Route
values: Notice, check, share via Prevent lead

teach.caption: Para 79: if someone is suspected of involvement in illegal terrorist-related activity, police should be informed immediately.

teach.body: Channel is a multi-agency programme, underpinned by s36 CTSA 2015, that supports people susceptible to becoming terrorists or supporting terrorism. It is voluntary: the person must consent. For a child under 18, consent is given by a parent, guardian or the agency responsible for their care (para 20). If consent is refused, Channel cannot proceed, but other safeguarding support for the child continues to be considered.

The nurse notices a pattern: repeated viewing of material glorifying an attack and extremist symbols. There is no threat or plan, so this is not a 999 situation. She checks by discussing it promptly with the trust's Prevent or safeguarding lead, records what she observed factually, and shares through a Prevent referral if the lead agrees. She continues to treat Callum with respect: Prevent is about supporting him, not punishing him.

teach.text: Prevent is not about one religion: it covers all ideologies, including extreme right-wing, and people increasingly mix ideas from different ideologies (para 27). And Channel is voluntary: for under-18s a parent, guardian or responsible agency consents.

items: NHS trusts must have due regard to preventing people being drawn into terrorism (CTSA 2015 s26).
Prevent duty guidance 2023, in force 31 December 2023; Prevent sits alongside safeguarding.
Notice, check (Prevent or safeguarding lead), share (Prevent referral).
Referrals screened by specialist police; Channel is multi-agency and voluntary.
Under 18: Channel consent from parent, guardian or responsible agency.
Imminent danger or terrorist activity: police immediately.

summary: You can now treat radicalisation as a safeguarding concern and apply notice, check, share through your Prevent lead. You can also explain the Channel process and consent for under-18s, and recognise when to call the police instead.

A.q: A student nurse asks what the Prevent duty requires of an NHS trust. Which statement is accurate?
options: Staff must report all religious conversion to police
Staff must screen every patient for extremist views
The trust must investigate any patient suspected of extremism
The trust must have due regard to preventing terrorism
A.why: CTSA 2015 s26: specified authorities, including NHS trusts, must have due regard to the need to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism.

whyNot.0: Religious conversion is not in itself a concern.
whyNot.1: There is no universal screening requirement.
whyNot.2: Investigation is a police role; health shares concerns.

A.q: A community children's nurse is uneasy after Aisha, 13, repeats extremist slogans she has seen online, but the nurse is unsure if this is a real concern. What is the best approach?
options: Wait to see if Aisha says anything more extreme
Notice, check and share through the Prevent lead
Call 999, as extremist slogans are a crime
Ask Aisha's school to monitor her behaviour closely
A.why: The guidance asks staff to notice, check (with the Prevent or safeguarding lead) and share concerns. Uncertainty is exactly why you check.

whyNot.2: There is no immediate danger requiring 999.
whyNot.3: Passing the concern to school bypasses the trust's Prevent route.

A.q: During training, a colleague says Prevent applies to Islamist extremism and not to Jack, 14, who is sharing far-right material. What is correct?
options: Prevent covers all forms, including extreme right-wing
Prevent covers far-right views after a criminal offence
Prevent covers Islamist ideology; far-right goes to police
Prevent covers adults; Jack goes to the school instead
A.why: The guidance deals with all kinds of terrorist threats, including Islamist and extreme right-wing ideologies.

whyNot.1: Prevent is preventive; no offence is needed.
whyNot.2: Extreme right-wing ideology is within Prevent.
whyNot.3: Prevent covers children as well as adults.

B.q: A Prevent referral about Zak, 14, is accepted for discussion at the local Channel panel. His mother asks whether he will be forced to take part. What is accurate?
options: Yes, as Channel is ordered by the police
Yes, as he is under 16 years old
No, at 14 he is old enough to make the decision himself
No, it is voluntary; a parent consents for him
B.why: Channel is voluntary. For under-18s, consent is given by a parent, guardian or the agency responsible for their care (para 20).

whyNot.0: Channel is not a police order.
whyNot.1: Age does not make Channel compulsory.
whyNot.2: For under-18s, consent comes from a parent, guardian or responsible agency.

B.q: During a night shift, Daniel, 16, tells a nurse he has bought chemicals online and will 'make the school pay' tomorrow morning. He shows her a photo of a device. What should she do first?
options: Make a Prevent referral via the Prevent lead tomorrow
Ask Daniel more about his plan to assess the risk
Contact the police immediately on 999
Inform the school's safeguarding lead by email
B.why: A specific plan with materials is an immediate danger. Police are informed immediately; safeguarding follows.

whyNot.0: A next-day referral is too slow for an imminent threat.
whyNot.3: Email is too slow for an imminent threat.

B.q: What happens to a Prevent referral after it is submitted?
options: The child is arrested and interviewed under caution
Specialist police assess it for possible Channel support
The NHS trust investigates the concern internally within 28 days
The school decides whether to exclude the child
B.why: Specialist police officers and staff assess referrals and decide whether there are reasonable grounds to consider the person for Channel (para 49).

whyNot.0: A Prevent referral is not an arrest.
whyNot.2: The trust shares concerns; it does not investigate.
whyNot.3: Exclusion is not part of the Prevent process.

C.q: After a Prevent referral, the Channel panel offers mentoring to Liam, 15. His parents refuse consent. The panel still believes Liam is vulnerable to radicalisation. What happens next?
options: Channel proceeds, as Liam's safety comes first
Channel proceeds if Liam himself agrees at 15
Channel cannot proceed; other support is considered
Channel cannot proceed, and Liam's case is closed by the panel
C.why: Channel is voluntary and needs consent from a parent, guardian or responsible agency for under-18s. Other safeguarding support for Liam continues to be considered.

whyNot.0: Channel cannot proceed without valid consent.
whyNot.1: For under-18s, consent comes from a parent, guardian or responsible agency.
whyNot.3: Liam's needs are still addressed through other safeguarding routes.

C.q: A newly qualified nurse is worried that a 15-year-old patient may be being radicalised by an older relative who visits. She is unsure who to speak to. Who should she contact first?
options: The relative, to understand his views
The Channel panel chair directly
The trust's Prevent or safeguarding lead
The local counter-terrorism policing unit directly
C.why: The 'check' step is a discussion with the organisation's Prevent or safeguarding lead, who can advise on a referral.

whyNot.0: Confronting the relative may increase risk.
whyNot.1: Channel receives cases after police assessment, not direct from ward staff.
whyNot.3: Direct police contact is for immediate danger; the trust route comes first.

C.q: Rosa, 14, has been looked after under a care order since last year. A Channel panel wants to offer her support. Who can give consent?
options: The agency responsible for her care, or a parent
Rosa herself, as she has been assessed as Gillick competent
The Channel panel chair on her behalf
The police officer who assessed the referral
C.why: For under-18s, consent is given by a parent, guardian or the agency that has responsibility for their care (para 20). Under a care order the local authority shares PR.

whyNot.1: The guidance places consent for under-18s with a parent, guardian or responsible agency.
whyNot.2: The panel cannot consent for her.
whyNot.3: Police assess referrals; they do not consent for the child.

reteach.title: Radicalisation is a safeguarding harm
reteach.question: How is Prevent different from reporting a crime?

blocks.body: Prevent works before any crime, to support children who may be drawn towards terrorism, much like protecting them from exploitation or grooming. You notice, check with your Prevent or safeguarding lead, and share. Specialist police assess the referral, and the Channel panel can offer voluntary support. Only a specific threat or terrorist activity means calling the police straight away.

blocks.text: All ideologies count. Channel is voluntary; for under-18s a parent, guardian or responsible agency consents.

explain.body: Specified authorities, including NHS trusts, must have due regard to the need to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism (CTSA 2015 s26). Guidance 2023 in force 31 December 2023.

test.q: What does 'due regard' mean in the Prevent duty guidance?
options: Reporting every concern directly to the police by phone
Giving appropriate weight to preventing terrorism
Making Prevent the trust's top priority
Screening all young patients at admission
test.why: Para 3: authorities should place an appropriate amount of weight on the need to prevent people becoming terrorists, alongside other relevant factors.

whyNot.0: Concerns go through notice, check, share, not direct to police by default.
whyNot.2: Due regard is appropriate weight, not overriding priority.

explain.body: Notice the concern; check with the Prevent or safeguarding lead; share through a Prevent referral if warranted.

test.q: In 'notice, check, share', what does 'check' involve for a ward nurse?
options: Searching the child's belongings
Asking the family about their beliefs
Reviewing the child's social media
Discussing it with the Prevent lead
test.why: Checking means discussing the concern with the organisation's Prevent or safeguarding lead.

whyNot.0: Searching belongings is not the nurse's role.
whyNot.1: Questioning the family may increase risk.
whyNot.2: Investigating online activity is not the nurse's role.

explain.body: Prevent deals with all terrorist threats, including Islamist and extreme right-wing ideologies; people may mix ideas from several ideologies.

test.q: A 15-year-old shares material combining ideas from several extremist ideologies. How does Prevent treat this?
options: As a recognised pattern within its scope
As outside scope, lacking one clear ideology
As a school discipline matter
As a mental health referral instead
test.why: Para 27 notes people increasingly adopt a mix of ideas from different ideologies; this remains within Prevent.

whyNot.1: A mixed or unclear ideology is still within Prevent.
whyNot.2: School discipline does not address radicalisation risk.
whyNot.3: Mental health support may help, but it does not replace Prevent.

explain.body: Multi-agency, voluntary support for people susceptible to radicalisation. Consent needed; for under-18s from a parent, guardian or responsible agency.

options: A police caution scheme for young offenders
A youth court diversion programme
A voluntary multi-agency support programme
A school exclusion review panel
test.why: Channel is a multi-agency programme providing voluntary support to people susceptible to becoming terrorists or supporting terrorism.

whyNot.0: Channel is not a caution scheme.
whyNot.1: Channel is not a court process.
whyNot.3: Channel is not an education panel.
